newsitem.title: INDIA: Investors cautiously cheer India core reforms.
newsitem.headline: Investors cautiously cheer India core reforms.

text.p: Foreign investors said on Thursday they were cheered by India's moves to attract private funds in roads, ports and telecommunications, but their optimism was tinged with caution.

"The measures definitely set a positive note and we fully support them... but what investors are asking us is, 'Do they really mean it? Are they going to implement these policies?'," said Rajiv Goel, consultant at auditing firm Coopers & Lybrand.
The Indian cabinet on Wednesday cleared several proposals to boost private investment in core sectors.
The moves include setting up an independent Infrastructure Development Finance Company (IDFC) to finance projects in areas such as power, roads, airports and railways.
The cabinet also approved the setting up of a telecommunications regulatory authority and an independent authority to decide tariffs for major ports.
It gave the go-ahead for a new policy on national highways which simplifies environmental clearances and allows investors to develop real estate along highways.
"The guidelines look good but the ground realities seem to be different," said Aditya Samant, economist at UBS Securities in Hong Kong.
"Investors would rather look at, say, the fight over the Tata-Singapore Airlines deal," Samant said.

A plan by India's Tata group and Singapore Airlines Ltd to set up a domestic airline recently cleared a major government hurdle, sparking an outcry among opposition leaders and Civil Aviation Minister C.M. Ibrahim.
Samant said the new announcements were a step in the right direction but unlikely to lead to any "immediate excitement".
"Investors are definitely going to look at what the government has to announce for the capital markets," he said.
In the last month, Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda has repeatedly promised a package to boost Indian capital markets and encourage investors to invest funds in its stock markets.

Bombay's benchmark stock index has jumped more than 30 percent in the past five weeks in response to these announcements, though it ended on Thursday down 5.3 percent to a provisional 3,453.61 points after soaring to 3,812.31 in morning trade.

Swarup Choudhury, manager corporate finance at HSBC Investment Banking in Bombay, said investors still had to regain confidence in the Indian government after a major power project by U.S. giant Enron Development Corp ran into trouble.

The 2,045 MW project was scrapped when a new rightwing government won elections in Maharashtra state in western India. After prolonged negotiations and more than 20 legal cases, Enron recently announced it was resuming work on the project.
"The Enron deal just showed that even after having a signed, sealed and delivered document, the government can backtrack," Choudhury said.
